source: Archaeobotany syntheses; package envelopes are directional evidence, not named-region rules. Wild-habitat envelopes are no longer carried here: W9 fits each package's envelope to its progenitors' observed occurrences (`crop-occurrences.json`) on a seasonal signature, and derives the range from it. W14 adds `standingWaterResponse`, the relative change of a package's monthly fit on ground standing under water: rice 1.0 (the paddy ~2x the upland crop: Bray 1986, *The Rice Economies*; GRiSP 2013, *Rice Almanac*, irrigated ~5.4 t/ha against rainfed lowland ~2.3 and upland ~1), the New Guinea roots 0.33 (taro's ~2x wet-over-dry gain, Kirch 1994, *The Wet and the Dry*, over one member of three), every other package -0.35 (the middle of the 20-50 % waterlogging loss in cereals, Setter & Waters 2003, Plant and Soil 253:1-34; the class figure applied to the tubers as well, coarse). W15: the positive responses are MANAGED-FLOODING yields — an irrigated paddy is bunded, levelled and transplanted; Kirch's wet taro is a built pondfield — so the positive half is scaled by the cultivator's technique and a wild stand gets none of it, while the negative half is physiology and applies at every technique. W17 adds `cycleDays`, the crop's own sowing-to-harvest cycle — how long it occupies the ground, which is the run of months whose weather sets the harvest. NOT `seasonMinimumMonths`, which is the minimum favourable season the crop needs to be grown here at all. From FAO-56 Table 11's total growing period (Allen, Pereira, Raes & Smith 1998, *Crop Evapotranspiration*, FAO Irrigation and Drainage Paper 56): the SHORTEST listed period among the package's own crops, because the sim's month-admission test already drops the months a crop cannot use, so a longer regional figure — long because of overwintering or cold dormancy — would count those months twice. Barley/Oats/Wheat 120 d (Central India, November); Rice 150 d (tropics and the Mediterranean); Maize (grain) 125 d (humid Nigeria, dry-cool India); Sorghum 130 d (USA, Pakistan, the Mediterranean); Millet 105 d (Pakistan, June); Cassava first year 210 d (rainy tropics); Squash/Zucchini 90 d (the Mediterranean and Europe, May/June sowing). The two the table omits are from the crops' own literature: enset 1460 d, the low end of the four-to-eight years to harvest maturity (Brandt et al. 1997, *The Tree Against Hunger*), which is over a year and so is graded by the year a perennial actually stands through; the New Guinea roots 210 d, the short end of greater yam's seven-to-ten months and dryland taro's seven-to-nine (Bourke & Harwood 2009, *Food and Agriculture in Papua New Guinea*, ch. 5). No value was tried against a gate row.
